DataTable.name: DataTable

unions.name: Column
unions.comment: Describes how to turn `data` into a column in your table.

unions.name: Config
unions.comment:
Configuration for your table, describing your columns.

**Note:** Your `Config` should _never_ be held in your model.
It should only appear in `view` code.

unions.name: SortDirection
unions.comment:
Simple boolean type for column sort direction. This type is not opaque and
meant to be used by other modules when constructing Table State

unions.name: Sorter
unions.comment: Specifies a particular way of sorting data.

unions.name: State
unions.comment:
Tracks which column to sort by, in which direction, the page size and the
position of the row cursor, as well as total number of rows of the whole
(possibly remote) table. This type is opaque.

aliases.name: Customizations
aliases.comment:
There are quite a lot of ways to customize the `<table>` tag. You can add
a `<caption>` which can be styled via CSS. You can do crazy stuff with
`<thead>` to group columns in weird ways. You can have a `<tfoot>` tag for
summaries of various columns. And maybe you want to put attributes on `<tbody>`
or on particular rows in the body. All these customizations are available to you.

**Note:** The level of craziness possible in `<thead>` and `<tfoot>` are so
high that I could not see how to provide the full functionality _and_ make it
impossible to do bad stuff. So just be aware of that, and share any stories
you have. Stories make it possible to design better!
aliases.type: { beforeAndAfterTable : { before : Maybe.Maybe (Html.Html msg), after : Maybe.Maybe (Html.Html msg) }, tableAttrs : Array.Array (Html.Attribute msg), caption : Maybe.Maybe (DataTable.HtmlDetails msg), colgroup : Array.Array (DataTable.HeaderInfo msg) -> Maybe.Maybe (DataTable.HtmlDetails msg), thead : Array.Array (DataTable.HeaderInfo msg) -> DataTable.HtmlDetails msg, tbodyAttrs : Array.Array (Html.Attribute msg), rowAttrs : (DataTable.State -> msg) -> DataTable.State -> data -> Array.Array (Html.Attribute msg), tfoot : Maybe.Maybe (DataTable.HtmlDetails msg) }

aliases.name: HtmlDetails
aliases.comment:
Sometimes you must use a `<td>` tag, but the attributes and children are up
to you. This type lets you specify all the details of an HTML node except the
tag name.
aliases.type: { attributes : Array.Array (Html.Attribute msg), children : Array.Array (Html.Html msg) }

values.name: column
values.type: ((data -> comparable) -> DataTable.Sorter data) -> String.String -> (data -> String.String) -> (data -> comparable) -> DataTable.Column data msg

values.name: config
values.comment:
Create the `Config` for your `view` function. Everything you need to
render your columns efficiently and handle selection of columns.

Say we have a `Array Person` that we want to show as a table. The table should
have a column for name and age. We would create a `Config` like this:

    import Table

    type Msg = NewTableState State | ...

    config : Table.Config Person Msg
    config =
      Table.config
        { toId = .name
        , toMsg = NewTableState
        , columns =
            [ Table.stringColumn "Name" .name
            , Table.intColumn "Age" .age
            ]
        }

You provide the following information in your table configuration:

  - `toId` — turn a `Person` into a unique ID. This lets us use
    [`Html.Keyed`][keyed] under the hood to make re-sorts faster.
  - `columns` — specify some columns to show.
  - `toMsg` — a way to send new table states to your app as messages.

See the [examples] to get a better feel for this!

[keyed]: http://package.elm-lang.org/packages/elm-lang/html/latest/Html-Keyed
[examples]: https://github.com/billstclair/elm-sortable-table/tree/master/examples
values.type: { toId : data -> String.String, toMsg : DataTable.State -> msg, columns : Array.Array (DataTable.Column data msg) } -> DataTable.Config data msg

values.name: customColumn
values.comment:
Perhaps the basic columns are not quite what you want. Maybe you want to
display monetary values in thousands of dollars, and `floatColumn` does not
quite cut it. You could define a custom column like this:

    import Table

    dollarColumn : String -> (data -> Float) -> Column data msg
    dollarColumn name toDollars =
        Table.customColumn
            { name = name
            , viewData = \data -> viewDollars (toDollars data)
            , sorter = Table.decreasingBy toDollars
            }

    viewDollars : Float -> String
    viewDollars dollars =
        "$" ++ String.fromInt (round (dollars / 1000)) ++ "k"

The `viewData` field means we will displays the number `12345.67` as `$12k`.

The `sorter` field specifies how the column can be sorted. In `dollarColumn` we
are saying that it can _only_ be shown from highest-to-lowest monetary value.
More about sorters soon!
values.type: { name : String.String, viewData : data -> String.String, sorter : DataTable.Sorter data } -> DataTable.Column data msg

values.name: customConfig
values.comment: Just like `config` but you can specify a bunch of table customizations.
values.type: { toId : data -> String.String, toMsg : DataTable.State -> msg, columns : Array.Array (DataTable.Column data msg), customizations : DataTable.Customizations data msg } -> DataTable.Config data msg

values.name: decreasingBy
values.comment:
Create a sorter that can only display the data in decreasing order. If we
want a table of countries, sorted by population from highest to lowest, we
would say this:

    sorter : Sorter { a | population : comparable }
    sorter =
        decreasingBy .population

values.name: decreasingOrIncreasingBy
values.comment:
Sometimes you want to be able to sort data in increasing _or_ decreasing
order. Maybe you have a bunch of data about orange juice, and you want to know
both which has the most sugar, and which has the least sugar. Both interesting!
This function lets you see both, starting with decreasing order.

    sorter : Sorter { a | sugar : comparable }
    sorter =
        decreasingOrIncreasingBy .sugar

values.name: defaultCustomizations
values.comment: The customizations used in `config` by default.

values.name: getPageSize
values.comment:
Inspect the current table state. What is the current page size for the
pagination. Showing "all rows" returns 0. This could be useful for storing
the sort state in a URL or somewhere else outside of Elm.

values.name: getRowCursor
values.comment:
Inspect the current table state. What is the current position of the row
cursor. Together with the current page size this determines which table page
is shown.

values.name: getSortState
values.comment:
Inspect the current table state. Which column is being sorted by, and
whether the sort order is ascending or descending. This could be useful for
storing the sort state in a URL or somewhere else outside of Elm.
values.type: DataTable.State -> Array.Array { sortColumnName : String.String, sortDirection : DataTable.SortDirection }

values.name: getSortedData
values.comment: Return the data sorted exactly as it will be displayed on the screen.
values.type: DataTable.Config data msg -> DataTable.State -> Array.Array data -> Array.Array data

values.name: increasingBy
values.comment:
Create a sorter that can only display the data in increasing order. If we
want a table of people, sorted alphabetically by name, we would say this:

    sorter : Sorter { a | name : comparable }
    sorter =
        increasingBy .name

values.name: increasingOrDecreasingBy
values.comment:
Sometimes you want to be able to sort data in increasing _or_ decreasing
order. Maybe you have race times for the 100 meter sprint. This function lets
sort by best time by default, but also see the other order.

    sorter : Sorter { a | time : comparable }
    sorter =
        increasingOrDecreasingBy .time

values.name: initialSort
values.comment:
Create an initial state for a table without pagination. By providing a column
name, you determine which column should be used for sorting by default. This is
meant to be used for simple tables. More
So if
you want your table of yachts to be sorted by length by default, you might say:

import Table

    Table.initialSort "Length"

values.name: new
values.comment:
Create a default table state. Only the id of the table is supplied. All other state is initialised with default values. This state can then be set with update functions. So if you wanted a table of countries that is by default sorted by population count in descending order you might write

import Table

    Table.new "Countries"
        |> DataTable.updateSortState "Population" DataTable.Desc

values.name: pageLength
values.type: DataTable.Config data msg -> DataTable.State -> Html.Html msg

values.name: unsortable
values.comment:
A sorter for columns that are unsortable. Maybe you have a column in your
table for delete buttons that delete the row. It would not make any sense to
sort based on that column.

values.name: veryCustomColumn
values.comment:
It is _possible_ that you want something crazier than `customColumn`. In
that unlikely scenario, this function lets you have full control over the
attributes and children of each `<td>` cell in this column.

So maybe you want to a dollars column, and the dollar signs should be green.

    import Html exposing (Attribute, Html, span, text)
    import Html.Attributes exposing (style)
    import Table

    dollarColumn : String -> (data -> Float) -> Column data msg
    dollarColumn name toDollars =
        Table.veryCustomColumn
            { name = name
            , viewData = \data -> viewDollars (toDollars data)
            , sorter = Table.decreasingBy toDollars
            }

    viewDollars : Float -> Table.HtmlDetails msg
    viewDollars dollars =
        Table.HtmlDetails []
            [ span [ style "color" "green" ] [ text "$" ]
            , text (String.fromInt (round (dollars / 1000)) ++ "k")
            ]
values.type: { name : String.String, viewData : data -> DataTable.HtmlDetails msg, sorter : DataTable.Sorter data } -> DataTable.Column data msg

values.name: view
values.comment:
Take a list of data and turn it into a table. The `Config` argument is the
configuration for the table. It describes the columns that we want to show. The
`State` argument describes which column we are sorting by at the moment.

**Note:** The `State` and `Array data` should live in your `Model`. The `Config`
for the table belongs in your `view` code. I very strongly recommend against
putting `Config` in your model. Describe any potential table configurations
statically, and look for a different library if you need something crazier than
that.
values.type: DataTable.Config data msg -> DataTable.State -> Array.Array data -> Html.Html msg
